facts_and_myths.explanation: Egas Moniz won the 1949 Nobel Prize in Medicine for developing the prefrontal lobotomy before safer psychotropic drugs replaced it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Motor control over fine hand and mouth movements occupies disproportionately large areas of the frontal motor cortex.

name: Hippocampus
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 cutaway of the brain's medial temporal lobe highlighting the curved seahorse-shaped hippocampus indexing memories.
core_traits: Curved seahorse-shaped neural structure located deep within the medial temporal lobe
Essential hub for converting short-term memories into long-term declarative memories (memory consolidation)
Contains specialized place cells that form cognitive spatial maps for navigation and mental orientation
One of the earliest and most severely affected brain regions in Alzheimer's disease pathology

facts_and_myths.claim: London taxi drivers develop an enlarged posterior hippocampus from memorizing thousands of city streets.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Neuroimaging showed taxi drivers who passed 'The Knowledge' navigation test had significantly greater gray matter volume in the hippocampus.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word hippocampus comes from Greek mythology, meaning 'sea horse' monster, due to its distinctive shape.

facts_and_myths.claim: Long-term memories are stored permanently inside the hippocampus like files on a hard drive.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The hippocampus acts as a temporary indexer; consolidated memories are eventually transferred to distributed areas of the cerebral cortex.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Patient H.M., whose hippocampi were surgically removed, could never form another new conscious memory for the rest of his life.

name: Amygdala
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 cinematic visualization of the paired almond-shaped amygdala glowing red deep in the limbic system during emotional threat detection.
core_traits: Paired almond-shaped clusters of nuclei nestled deep within the brain's temporal lobes
Key component of the limbic system responsible for processing emotions, especially fear and aggression
Orchestrates rapid physiological threat detection and triggers immediate fight-or-flight signaling
Plays an essential role in emotional memory consolidation and reading emotional facial expressions

facts_and_myths.claim: People with bilateral destruction of the amygdala experience almost total fearlessness.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Patient S.M., who has Urbach-Wiethe disease destroying both amygdalae, exhibits complete lack of fear toward snakes, spiders, and horror films.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word amygdala derives from the Greek word for 'almond', matching its size and outline.

facts_and_myths.claim: The amygdala is solely a destructive center producing negative anger and phobias.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The amygdala processes all biologically salient stimuli, including positive social rewards, romance, affection, and joyful excitement.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: An 'amygdala hijack' occurs when emotional threat circuits bypass logical prefrontal reasoning during sudden rage or panic.

name: Peripheral Nerves
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 luminous anatomical web showing peripheral nerve branches spreading from the central spine into limbs and fingertips.
core_traits: Vast network of cable-like nerve bundles branching outside the brain and spinal cord
Connects the central nervous system (CNS) to the limbs, skin, skeletal muscles, and internal organs
Composed of 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves
Divided functionally into somatic (voluntary motor and sensory) and autonomic nervous divisions

facts_and_myths.claim: Unlike central nervous system nerves, severed peripheral nerves have the biological ability to regrow.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Schwann cells in peripheral nerves produce nerve growth factors, allowing cut axons to regenerate at roughly 1 millimeter per day.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The pins and needles sensation (paresthesia) happens when sustained physical pressure starves peripheral nerves of blood flow.

facts_and_myths.claim: Peripheral nerves contain only one-way motor wires that carry commands from brain to muscle.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Most peripheral nerves are mixed nerves, carrying both afferent sensory data toward the spinal cord and efferent motor instructions out.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an autoimmune attack on the myelin insulation of peripheral nerves, causing temporary paralysis.

name: Sciatic Nerve
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of the thick sciatic nerve descending from the lower lumbar spine through the pelvis down the leg.
core_traits: Longest and widest single nerve in the entire human body
Originates from spinal roots L4 through S3 in the lumbosacral plexus
Travels from the lower back through the buttock down the posterior thigh to the foot
Measures approximately as thick as an adult human thumb at its widest pelvic origin

facts_and_myths.claim: Sciatica is caused by irritation, inflammation, or pinching of the sciatic nerve roots.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A herniated disc or bone spur in the lumbar spine compressing the nerve causes shooting electric pain radiating down the leg.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Near the popliteal fossa behind the knee, the sciatic nerve splits into the tibial and common fibular nerves.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sciatic nerve pain always originates from a muscular tear directly in the calf muscle.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While pain can radiate into the calf and foot, the structural root cause is almost always in the lower lumbar spine or piriformis muscle.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sitting on a thick wallet in your back pocket can compress the sciatic nerve, a condition nicknamed 'wallet sciatica'.

name: Vagus Nerve
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical visual of the extensive wandering vagus nerve meandering from the brainstem into the heart, lungs, and intestines.
core_traits: Tenth cranial nerve (CN X) and the longest cranial nerve in the human body
Originates in the brainstem and wanders extensively into the neck, chest, heart, lungs, and gut
Primary commander of the parasympathetic nervous system governing the rest-and-digest response
Slows heart rate, stimulates digestive enzyme secretion, and moderates systemic inflammation

facts_and_myths.claim: Overstimulation of the vagus nerve can cause a sudden drop in heart rate and fainting (vasovagal syncope).
facts_and_myths.explanation: Triggers like sight of blood, extreme fear, or prolonged standing cause acute vagal surges, pooling blood in legs and fainting.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word vagus comes from the Latin word for 'wandering', the same root as 'vagrant' and 'vagabond'.

facts_and_myths.claim: The vagus nerve carries signals in only one direction from the brain down to abdominal organs.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Roughly 80 percent of vagus nerve fibers are afferent (sensory), sending gut microbiome and organ data upward into the brain.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) devices are surgically implanted to treat drug-resistant epilepsy and severe depression.

name: Autonomic Nervous System
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 duality graphic illustrating the twin branches of the autonomic system: red fight-or-flight vs blue rest-and-digest.
core_traits: Division of the peripheral nervous system regulating involuntary physiological body functions
Controls heart rate, digestion, respiration rate, salivation, perspiration, and pupillary dilation
Divided into two antagonistic branches: sympathetic (fight-or-flight) and parasympathetic (rest-and-digest)
Maintains continuous internal physiological stability known as homeostasis

facts_and_myths.claim: The autonomic nervous system can be consciously influenced through controlled slow deep breathing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Prolonged exhalation activates the parasympathetic vagus nerve, deliberately lowering heart rate and reducing stress hormones.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The enteric nervous system embedded in the gut is often classified as a semi-autonomous third branch of the ANS.

facts_and_myths.claim: Humans can completely shut down their autonomic nervous system through deep meditation.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Total shutdown of autonomic function would stop the heartbeat and respiration, causing immediate clinical death.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pupil dilation in the dark is mediated by sympathetic nerves, while constriction in bright sun is parasympathetic.

name: Sensory Neurons
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 macro perspective of sensory pseudounipolar neurons gathering touch, thermal, and pain cues from peripheral skin receptors.
core_traits: Nerve cells that convert external environmental stimuli into internal electrical impulses
Carry afferent sensory information from sensory receptors toward the central nervous system
Equipped with specialized receptor endings detecting touch, temperature, light, sound, taste, or pain
Cell bodies of somatic sensory neurons reside in the dorsal root ganglia just outside the spinal cord

facts_and_myths.claim: Sensory neurons in the fingertip can detect surface textures with microscopic ridges less than a single hair's width.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Meissner's corpuscles and Merkel discs can detect nanoscale surface vibrations and friction down to 13 nanometers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Nociceptive sensory neurons specifically transmit signals warning of potential or actual tissue trauma (pain).

facts_and_myths.claim: Sensory neurons are physically identical to motor neurons in structural morphology.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Most sensory neurons are pseudounipolar, possessing a single axon that splits in two, whereas motor neurons are multipolar.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pain signals travel along two types of sensory fibers: fast myelinated A-delta fibers (sharp pain) and slow unmyelinated C fibers (dull ache).

name: Motor Neurons
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of a motor neuron axon terminating at a glowing neuromuscular junction across muscle fiber striations.
core_traits: Nerve cells originating in the spinal cord and brainstem that project axons to target muscles and glands
Carry efferent motor commands from the central nervous system to stimulate muscular contraction
Interface directly with skeletal muscle fibers at specialized chemical synapses called neuromuscular junctions
Release acetylcholine to trigger muscle cell depolarization and calcium-mediated contraction

facts_and_myths.claim: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, Lou Gehrig's disease) selectively attacks and destroys motor neurons.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In ALS, upper and lower motor neurons degenerate, preventing the brain from initiating and controlling voluntary muscle movement.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Stephen Hawking famously lived for over five decades with an unusually slow-progressing motor neuron disease.

facts_and_myths.claim: Each individual motor neuron connects to every single muscle fiber across an entire muscle group.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A single motor neuron innervates a specific group of fibers, forming a 'motor unit'; delicate eye muscles have units of just 3 to 5 fibers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Upper motor neurons reside in the cerebral cortex, while lower motor neurons sit in the spinal cord's anterior horns.

name: Blood
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 microscopic stream of rich crimson blood surging through a transparent vessel carrying glowing cellular elements.
core_traits: Specialized liquid connective tissue circulating continuously throughout the cardiovascular system
An average adult possesses approximately 5 liters (about 1.2 to 1.5 gallons) of blood
Composed of 55 percent liquid plasma and 45 percent formed elements (erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets)
Transports oxygen, nutrients, metabolic wastes, hormones, and immune defenses to every body tissue

facts_and_myths.claim: Deoxygenated human blood inside veins is naturally bright royal blue in color.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Human blood is never blue; oxygenated blood is bright cherry red, and deoxygenated blood is deep dark red. Veins look blue due to light skin scattering.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Horseshoe crabs have genuinely bright blue blood because their oxygen carrier uses copper (hemocyanin) instead of iron.

facts_and_myths.claim: Blood accounts for roughly 7 to 8 percent of total human adult body weight.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In an adult weighing 70 kilograms (154 pounds), circulating blood accounts for roughly 5 to 5.5 kilograms.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It takes only about 20 to 60 seconds for a single drop of blood to complete a full circuit through the entire human body.

name: Red Blood Cells
visual_anchor: Microscopic vertical 9:16 visual of flexible biconcave disc red blood cells gliding single-file through a tight capillary bed.
core_traits: Most abundant cellular component of human blood, making up about 40 to 45 percent of blood volume
Distinctive biconcave disc shape optimizing surface area for rapid gas diffusion
Filled with hundreds of millions of iron-rich hemoglobin molecules that bind oxygen
Lacks a cell nucleus and mitochondria at maturity, maximizing internal oxygen storage space

facts_and_myths.claim: Mature human red blood cells do not contain DNA or a cell nucleus.
facts_and_myths.explanation: During maturation in the bone marrow, mammalian erythrocytes eject their nuclei to maximize space for hemoglobin.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Because they lack a nucleus and repair machinery, red blood cells live for only about 120 days before being recycled by the spleen.

facts_and_myths.claim: Red blood cells consume large portions of the oxygen they transport to power their own internal mitochondria.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Erythrocytes have zero mitochondria; they generate ATP strictly through anaerobic glycolysis, delivering 100 percent of oxygen cargo.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Your body produces roughly 2 million new red blood cells every single second in the bone marrow.

name: White Blood Cells
visual_anchor: Microscopic vertical 9:16 action render of an amoeboid white blood cell engulfing glowing green bacteria through phagocytosis.
core_traits: Mobile cellular soldiers of the immune system defending against infectious pathogens and foreign invaders
Makes up approximately 1 percent of healthy circulating blood volume
Five major classes: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils
Capable of diapedesis - crawling directly out of capillary blood vessels into infected surrounding tissue

facts_and_myths.claim: Pus forming at an infected wound site consists primarily of dead white blood cells.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Neutrophils rush to the infection, engulf bacteria, and die in huge numbers, creating the thick yellowish fluid called pus.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Neutrophils make up about 60 to 70 percent of all circulating white blood cells.

facts_and_myths.claim: Having an extremely high white blood cell count is always a healthy sign of supreme immunity.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Severely elevated counts (leukocytosis) signal active infection, severe inflammation, or hematologic cancers like leukemia.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Lymphocytes include B-cells (which manufacture antibodies) and T-cells (which destroy virus-infected cells).

name: Platelets
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 macro perspective of activated spiky platelets weaving a dense golden fibrin mesh to plug a bleeding vessel wall.
core_traits: Tiny disc-shaped cell fragments circulating in the blood vital for hemostasis (blood clotting)
Pinched off from giant precursor cells in the bone marrow known as megakaryocytes
Lacks a cell nucleus, with an average circulating lifespan of only 8 to 10 days
Adheres to exposed collagen at injury sites, activating and releasing clotting factors to form plugs

facts_and_myths.claim: A single drop of healthy human blood contains tens of thousands of platelets.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Normal platelet counts range from 150,000 to 450,000 platelets per microliter of blood.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hemophilia is a genetic disorder where clotting factor deficiencies prevent stable platelet-fibrin clots from forming.

facts_and_myths.claim: Platelets are fully formed independent living cells with their own genetic nuclei.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Platelets are not true whole cells; they are anucleate cytoplasmic fragments shed into the circulation by megakaryocytes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When activated, platelets change shape from smooth plates into starburst spheres with extended grasping tentacles.

name: Blood Plasma
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 visual of centrifuged blood separating into yellow liquid plasma at the top and dense crimson cells at the base.
core_traits: Straw-colored liquid matrix of blood making up approximately 55 percent of total blood volume
Composed of approximately 92 percent water, 7 percent vital proteins, and 1 percent dissolved solutes
Key plasma proteins include albumin (maintaining osmotic pressure), globulins (antibodies), and fibrinogen (clotting)
Carries dissolved glucose, amino acids, electrolytes, hormones, and dissolved carbon dioxide

facts_and_myths.claim: Donated blood plasma can be frozen and safely stored for up to a full calendar year.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) is stored at minus 18 degrees Celsius or colder, preserving delicate clotting factors for 12 months.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Albumin in plasma acts like a sponge, holding water inside blood vessels so it doesn't leak into body tissues.

facts_and_myths.claim: Blood serum and blood plasma are chemically identical terms with zero physiological difference.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Plasma contains all clotting factors including fibrinogen; serum is the liquid left over after blood has completely clotted.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Plasma donations are widely used to manufacture lifesaving intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) for immune-deficient patients.

name: Hemoglobin
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 molecular visualization of the four-subunit quaternary hemoglobin protein cradling glowing red iron heme groups.
core_traits: Iron-containing metalloprotein found inside red blood cells responsible for oxygen transport
Tetrameric protein composed of four globular protein subunits, each containing an iron-bearing heme ring
Can bind up to four molecules of oxygen reversibly to form bright red oxyhemoglobin
Also transports roughly 20 percent of cellular metabolic carbon dioxide waste as carbaminohemoglobin

facts_and_myths.claim: Carbon monoxide is lethal because it binds to hemoglobin over 200 times more tightly than oxygen.
facts_and_myths.explanation: CO outcompetes oxygen for heme binding sites, locking the molecule and causing severe cellular asphyxiation without any smell or warning.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The iron atom in heme binds oxygen, which is what gives blood its bright red color.

facts_and_myths.claim: Eating spinach supplies more iron than red meat because Popeye proved it maximizes hemoglobin.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The famous iron content of spinach was inflated by a decimal error in early studies; non-heme plant iron is absorbed less efficiently than meat heme iron.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sickle cell disease is caused by a single point mutation changing one amino acid in the beta-globin chain of hemoglobin.

name: Arteries
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 cutaway of a thick-walled muscular artery pulsating with high-pressure oxygenated blood from the heart.
core_traits: High-pressure blood vessels that carry oxygenated blood away from the heart to body tissues
Possess thick, elastic, and muscular walls made of three layers (tunica intima, media, and externa)
Expand and recoil rhythmically with each ventricular contraction, producing the palpable pulse
Branch into smaller resistance vessels called arterioles that regulate systemic blood pressure

facts_and_myths.claim: Every single artery in the human body carries bright, fully oxygenated blood.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the heart directly to the lungs to pick up oxygen.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Arteries are defined strictly by flow direction (away from heart), not by blood oxygen saturation.

facts_and_myths.claim: Arteries have their own tiny network of blood vessels supplying their outer muscular walls.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Large arteries are so thick that oxygen cannot diffuse through their walls; they are fed by micro-vessels called the vasa vasorum.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ancient Greek anatomists found arteries empty after death and mistakenly believed they transported air, hence 'arteria' (air conveyor).

name: Veins
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of a translucent blue vein showing crescent-shaped one-way pocket valves preventing blood backflow.
core_traits: Low-pressure capacitance blood vessels that transport deoxygenated blood back toward the heart
Equipped with internal one-way flap valves to prevent backward pooling of blood against gravity
Possess thinner muscular walls and wider lumens than companion arteries
Rely heavily on the surrounding skeletal muscle pump and respiratory pressure changes to propel blood

facts_and_myths.claim: Varicose veins occur when the tiny internal one-way valves inside leg veins fail and leak.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When venous valves become incompetent, gravity causes blood to pool and back up, stretching veins into swollen, twisted cords.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: At any given moment, roughly 65 to 70 percent of your total blood volume resides resting inside the systemic venous system.

facts_and_myths.claim: Blood flowing through arm and leg veins is literally bright blue in color.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Venous blood is dark burgundy-red; veins appear blue through skin because blue light wavelengths reflect while red penetrates.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The pulmonary veins are unique among veins because they carry freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

name: Capillaries
visual_anchor: Microscopic vertical 9:16 visual of a microscopic capillary network where red blood cells squeeze through single file to exchange oxygen.
core_traits: Smallest and most numerous blood vessels in the human body, bridging arterioles and venules
Possess walls composed of only a single layer of endothelial cells, thinner than a plastic wrap
Site of all physiological gas, nutrient, fluid, and waste exchange between blood and interstitial tissues
Diameter is so narrow (5 to 10 micrometers) that red blood cells must deform and pass through single-file

facts_and_myths.claim: If you unraveled all the capillaries in a single adult human, they would circle the Earth over two times.
facts_and_myths.explanation: There are approximately 10 billion capillaries totaling roughly 60,000 to 100,000 miles (100,000 km) in length.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Blood flows through capillaries at a leisurely crawl (under 1 mm/s) to give ample time for nutrient diffusion.

facts_and_myths.claim: Capillaries are lined with thick smooth muscle bands that contract to pump blood forward.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Capillaries have zero muscle tissue in their walls; flow is regulated upstream by precapillary sphincters on metarterioles.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The cornea of the eye and cartilage tissue are among the few vascular structures in the human body lacking capillaries.

name: Aorta
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 anatomical view of the massive candy-cane-shaped aorta arching gracefully out of the left ventricle of the heart.
core_traits: Largest and thickest blood vessel in the entire human body
Originates directly from the heart's left ventricle, carrying high-pressure oxygenated blood
Arches like a candy cane (aortic arch) before descending through the chest and abdomen
Measures over an inch (2.5 to 3 centimeters) in diameter in healthy adults

facts_and_myths.claim: The elastic recoil of the aorta keeps blood flowing smoothly even while the heart is resting between beats.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Known as the Windkessel effect, the elastic aortic wall expands under systolic pressure and recoils during diastole, damping pulses.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A tear in the inner layer of the aorta (aortic dissection) is one of the most lethal medical emergencies known.

facts_and_myths.claim: The aorta carries deoxygenated blood directly to the lungs for gas exchange.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The pulmonary artery feeds the lungs; the aorta distributes rich oxygenated blood to all systemic organs and peripheral tissues.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Branches off the aortic arch supply the head and arms: the brachiocephalic, left common carotid, and left subclavian arteries.

name: Vena Cava
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical render of the superior and inferior vena cava vessels channeling dark deoxygenated blood into the right atrium.
core_traits: Two largest systemic veins in the human body returning deoxygenated blood to the right atrium
Superior Vena Cava (SVC) drains blood from the head, neck, arms, and upper chest
Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) drains blood from the lower limbs, pelvis, and abdominal organs
Runs vertically parallel to the abdominal aorta along the posterior abdominal wall

facts_and_myths.claim: The inferior vena cava is the largest single vein by diameter in the human body.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The IVC measures up to 3.5 centimeters (1.4 inches) in diameter, carrying all venous return from below the diaphragm.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pregnant women in late pregnancy are advised to sleep on their left side to prevent the heavy uterus from compressing the IVC.

facts_and_myths.claim: The vena cava contains thick muscular pumping chambers similar to the ventricles of the heart.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The vena cava is a passive conduit with thin walls lacking intrinsic pumping power; blood moves via thoracic suction and muscle pumps.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Unlike veins in the legs, the large vena cava has no internal valves.

name: Coronary Arteries
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 cinematic visual of left and right coronary arteries branching like a crown across the pulsing myocardium surface.
core_traits: Specialized arterial blood vessels branching directly from the base of the ascending aorta
Encircle the heart like a crown, supplying oxygen-rich blood directly to the working heart muscle (myocardium)
Left Main and Right Coronary Arteries divide into major branches including the LAD (left anterior descending)
Susceptible to atherosclerotic plaque accumulation that causes ischemic coronary artery disease

facts_and_myths.claim: The left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery is nicknamed the 'widowmaker'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because the LAD supplies over 50 percent of the left ventricle, an acute blockage causes catastrophic, often fatal myocardial infarction.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Coronary arteries fill with blood primarily during cardiac diastole (when the heart relaxes), unlike other systemic arteries.

facts_and_myths.claim: The heart muscle gets all its oxygen directly by absorbing blood flowing inside its own four interior chambers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The thick muscular myocardium cannot absorb oxygen across its endocardium lining; it relies exclusively on external coronary arteries.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Coronary bypass surgery (CABG) often harvests the saphenous vein from the leg to detour around blocked coronary arteries.

name: Blood Vessels
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 full-body transparent silhouette illuminated by a glowing scarlet circulatory web of 60,000 miles of blood vessels.
core_traits: Closed tubular highway network transporting blood to and from every tissue in the body
Includes five primary classifications: arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, and veins
Lined with a continuous smooth single layer of endothelial cells regulating clotting and vessel tone
Total combined length in an adult human measures roughly 60,000 to 100,000 miles

facts_and_myths.claim: Blood vessels can dynamically widen (vasodilation) and narrow (vasoconstriction) to regulate body temperature.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When hot, skin blood vessels dilate to radiate heat; when freezing, they constrict to conserve core warm blood for vital organs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Blushing is an involuntary emotional vasodilation of facial blood vessels triggered by sympathetic nervous surges.

facts_and_myths.claim: Blood vessels are rigid, static plumbing pipes that never remodel or sprout new branches.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Through angiogenesis, new blood vessels sprout continuously to heal wounds, accommodate muscle growth, and adapt to exercise.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Atherosclerosis (hardening of the arteries) can begin developing in blood vessels as early as late childhood.

name: Lymph Nodes
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of bean-shaped lymph nodes clustered along glowing lymphatic vessels in the neck and armpit.
core_traits: Small, bean-shaped immune filtration checkpoints situated along lymphatic vessels
Humans have approximately 500 to 700 lymph nodes clustered in the neck, armpits, groin, and abdomen
Packed with immune lymphocytes and macrophages that trap and destroy bacteria, viruses, and cancer cells
Filter interstitial lymph fluid before returning it safely to the venous bloodstream

facts_and_myths.claim: Swollen tender lymph nodes in the neck indicate your immune system is actively fighting off an infection.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lymphocytes multiply rapidly inside the node to mount an antibody response, causing the node to enlarge and feel tender.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Surgeons remove the 'sentinel lymph node' during breast cancer surgery to check if metastatic cells have spread.

facts_and_myths.claim: Lymph nodes are endocrine hormone glands identical to the thyroid and pituitary glands.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lymph nodes secrete zero hormones; they are immune filtration filters, which is why calling them 'lymph glands' is a misnomer.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Lymph fluid moves through nodes via body movement and muscular contraction, as the lymphatic system has no central pump.

name: Lymphatic System
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical illustration showing the green-tinted glowing network of lymphatic vessels draining interstitial fluid into the thoracic duct.
core_traits: Extensive network of drainage vessels, lymphoid organs, and tissues operating parallel to the circulatory system
Collects excess interstitial fluid leaked from blood capillaries and returns roughly 3 liters daily to venous blood
Transports dietary fats absorbed in the small intestine via specialized milky lymph vessels called lacteals
Includes lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils, bone marrow, and the massive thoracic duct

facts_and_myths.claim: Elephantiasis is caused by parasitic worms blocking the drainage vessels of the lymphatic system.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Filarial worms lodge in lymphatic vessels, causing severe chronic lymphedema and massive swelling in legs and tissues.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The brain has its own specialized waste drainage network called the glymphatic system, active mostly during sleep.

facts_and_myths.claim: The lymphatic system possesses an independent muscular heart to pump lymph throughout the body.
facts_and_myths.explanation: There is no lymph heart; lymph flows strictly via smooth muscle contraction in vessel walls, skeletal muscle movement, and breathing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: All lymph from the lower body and left upper body drains into the thoracic duct, which empties into the left subclavian vein.

name: Bone Marrow
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 cross-sectional view of the interior hollow of a femur bone revealing spongy red marrow generating blood stem cells.
core_traits: Soft, spongy, flexible tissue filling the interior cavities and trabecular spaces of bones
Site of hematopoiesis - the production of all red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets
Exists in two forms: red marrow (actively producing blood) and yellow marrow (storing adipose fat)
Houses hematopoietic stem cells capable of lifelong self-renewal and multilineage differentiation

facts_and_myths.claim: A bone marrow transplant can change a recipient's circulating blood type to match the donor's blood type.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because donor stem cells take over blood cell production completely, the recipient's new red blood cells express the donor's ABO type.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: All bone marrow is red at birth, but with age, roughly half converts into fatty yellow marrow.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bone marrow stem cells can only ever be harvested through painful drilling into the pelvic hip bone.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Over 80 percent of modern stem cell donations are collected non-surgically from circulating blood via peripheral blood apheresis.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In extreme starvation, yellow bone marrow fat is the very last adipose tissue the body consumes for survival.

name: Human Skeleton
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 anatomical view of the full human skeleton standing in dynamic pose illuminated by crisp studio rim lighting.
core_traits: Internal rigid framework of mineralized bones supporting and shaping the human body
Adult human skeleton consists of 206 named bones; infants are born with roughly 270 bones
Divided into axial skeleton (skull, spine, ribs: 80 bones) and appendicular skeleton (limbs, girdles: 126 bones)
Protects vital internal organs, anchors muscles for movement, and stores 99 percent of body calcium

facts_and_myths.claim: Human babies are born with significantly more individual bones than fully grown adults.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Infants have roughly 270 flexible cartilaginous bone elements that gradually fuse together during growth into the adult 206 bones.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: More than half of all the 206 bones in the adult human skeleton are located in the hands and feet alone (106 bones).

facts_and_myths.claim: Bones are dry, dead structural calcified rods that never change once you reach adulthood.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Bone is living dynamic tissue; osteoclasts and osteoblasts continuously remodel the skeleton, completely replacing it every 10 years.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ounce for ounce, human cortical bone has greater tensile strength and compressive strength than reinforced concrete.

name: Skull
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical render of the human skull with cranial suture lines highlighted and deep eye orbits gazing forward.
core_traits: Bony structure forming the head that encases and protects the brain and supports facial anatomy
Composed of 22 individual bones: 8 cranial bones and 14 facial skeleton bones
Cranial bones are joined together by immovable interlocking fibrous joints called sutures
The mandible (lower jawbone) is the only freely movable bone in the adult skull

facts_and_myths.claim: Newborn human babies possess soft spots on their skulls where bones have not yet fused.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fontanelles allow the infant skull to deform safely through the birth canal and expand rapidly as the brain doubles in size.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The anterior fontanelle on top of a baby's head typically closes completely between 12 and 18 months of age.

facts_and_myths.claim: The human skull is a single solid monolithic dome of bone formed without seams.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The cranium is assembled from separate plates (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital) united by zigzagging suture lines.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The foramen magnum is the large oval opening at the base of the skull where the brainstem exits into the spinal cord.

name: Spine
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 visual of the S-curved vertebral column showing alternating stacked bone vertebrae and glowing intervertebral discs.
core_traits: Flexible bony column composed of 33 stacked vertebrae extending from the skull base to the pelvis
Divided into 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, and 4 fused coccygeal vertebrae
Features natural cervical, thoracic, and lumbar S-curves that absorb vertical shock and maintain upright posture
Surrounds and protects the delicate spinal cord within the central neural canal

facts_and_myths.claim: Humans are measurably taller in the morning immediately after waking up than in the evening.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Gravity compresses the gel-filled intervertebral discs throughout the day; lying down allows them to rehydrate and expand up to 1 cm.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Humans and giraffes both have the exact same number of cervical neck vertebrae: precisely seven.

facts_and_myths.claim: A healthy human spine is completely straight like an iron ruler when viewed from the side.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A healthy spine has four natural lordotic and kyphotic curves; a completely straight spine would lack shock absorption and break easily.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The coccyx at the base of the spine represents the vestigial evolutionary remnant of an ancestral mammalian tail.

name: Rib Cage
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of the curved rib cage enclosing glowing silhouettes of heart and lungs attached to the sternum.
core_traits: Bony and cartilaginous basket protecting vital heart, lungs, and liver in the thoracic cavity
Composed of 12 pairs of ribs (24 total), the central sternum, and 12 thoracic vertebrae
Divided into 7 true ribs (attaching directly to sternum), 3 false ribs, and 2 floating ribs
Expands and contracts rhythmically during breathing assisted by intercostal muscles

facts_and_myths.claim: Men have one fewer rib than women because God removed Adam's rib to create Eve.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Anatomically, both men and women almost universally possess exactly 12 pairs (24 total) of ribs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Roughly 1 in 200 people are born with a harmless extra cervical rib growing from the seventh neck vertebra.

facts_and_myths.claim: The bottom two pairs of ribs are called 'floating ribs' because they have zero anterior sternal attachment.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Ribs 11 and 12 attach only to vertebrae at the back, ending freely in abdominal muscle walls without cartilage reaching the front.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Costal cartilage connecting ribs to the sternum allows the chest to flex and absorb forceful impacts without shattering.

name: Pelvis
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of the basin-shaped pelvis highlighting the flared ilium wings and deep hip acetabulum sockets.
core_traits: Basin-shaped ring of bones connecting the vertebral spine to the lower appendicular limbs
Composed of two hip bones (each formed by fused ilium, ischium, and pubis) plus the sacrum and coccyx
Features deep cup-shaped sockets (acetabula) forming the mobile ball-and-socket hip joints with femurs
Supports upper body weight, protects pelvic viscera, and anchors powerful core and leg muscles

facts_and_myths.claim: Forensic anthropologists can reliably determine biological sex from skeletal pelvis shape.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The female pelvis evolved a wider, shallower basin, a broader pubic arch, and a larger circular inlet to facilitate childbirth.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word pelvis is the direct Latin word for 'basin', describing its bowl-like shape perfectly.

facts_and_myths.claim: The three bones of the hip (ilium, ischium, and pubis) remain separate movable pieces throughout adult life.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They fuse together completely by late adolescence to form a single solid os coxae (hip bone) on each side.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The obturator foramen in the pelvis is the largest natural hole in the human skeleton.

name: Femur
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 render of the massive human femur bone showing its spherical ball head and dense cortical shaft.
core_traits: Longest, heaviest, and strongest bone in the entire human skeleton
Spans the upper leg from the hip joint to the knee joint
Features a prominent spherical head fitting snugly into the pelvic acetabulum
Capable of supporting up to 30 times an adult human's body weight in compressive force

facts_and_myths.claim: A human femur bone is stronger and more resilient than an equivalent weight of concrete.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Its dense hollow cylindrical architecture and collagen-hydroxyapatite composite matrix give it exceptional compressive and bending strength.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: An adult femur accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total standing height.

facts_and_myths.claim: When an elderly person 'breaks their hip', the bone that actually fractures is the pelvic socket.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Most 'hip fractures' are fractures of the femoral neck just below the ball head of the femur, not the pelvic bone.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fracturing a femur requires extreme violent force, such as a high-speed car crash or fall from great height.

name: Humerus
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of the long cylindrical humerus bone connecting the shoulder scapula to the forearm elbow.
core_traits: Single long bone of the upper arm connecting the shoulder to the elbow joint
Articulates proximally with the glenoid cavity of the scapula forming the shoulder joint
Articulates distally with the radius and ulna to form the hinge-pivot elbow complex
Anchors major arm and chest muscles including the deltoid, pectoralis major, biceps, and triceps

facts_and_myths.claim: Hitting your 'funny bone' is actually an impact against the humerus bone tissue itself.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The funny bone sensation is not a bone at all; it is the ulnar nerve getting pinched against the medial epicondyle of the humerus.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The English word 'humerus' is anatomically homophonous with 'humorous', which popularized the 'funny bone' pun.

facts_and_myths.claim: The ball head of the humerus sits in a much shallower socket than the femur, trading stability for range of motion.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The shoulder glenoid fossa covers only one-third of the humerus head, making it the most mobile - and most easily dislocated - joint in the body.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The radial groove spiraling along the humerus shaft carries the radial nerve controlling wrist extension.

name: Tibia
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical perspective of the stout triangular tibia bone bearing weight in the lower front leg.
core_traits: Larger, stronger, and more anterior of the two lower leg bones
Second longest and second strongest bone in the entire human skeleton
Primary weight-bearing bone of the lower leg, supporting virtually all body weight above the ankle
Anterior border forms the prominent sharp ridge felt directly under the skin as the shin

facts_and_myths.claim: The shin is exceptionally sensitive to impact because the tibia's front border has no muscle padding.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The anterior border of the tibia sits directly beneath the skin with only periosteum covering it, leaving pain-sensing nerves exposed.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ancient Romans carved musical flutes from animal shinbones, which is where the Latin word 'tibia' (flute) originated.

facts_and_myths.claim: The tibia and fibula bear equal halves of a person's standing body weight.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The stout tibia carries over 85 to 90 percent of body weight; the slender fibula acts mainly as a muscle anchor and ankle stabilizer.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The medial malleolus forming the prominent inner ankle bump is the distal end of the tibia.

name: Fibula
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical cutaway highlighting the slender toothpick-like fibula running parallel along the outer side of the tibia.
core_traits: Slender long bone positioned on the lateral (outer) side of the lower leg parallel to the tibia
Thinnest of all long bones in the human body relative to its total length
Does not articulate with the femur or participate directly in the weight-bearing knee joint
Distal end expands to form the lateral malleolus, the prominent bump on the outer ankle

facts_and_myths.claim: Surgeons can harvest segments of the fibula for bone graft reconstructions without impairing walking.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because the fibula bears very little weight, sections of its middle shaft can be safely transplanted to rebuild jaws or arms.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word fibula comes from Latin for 'clasp' or 'brooch pin', describing how it pins against the larger tibia.

facts_and_myths.claim: A fractured fibula leaves a person completely unable to place any weight on the leg.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because the tibia carries nearly all body weight, some individuals can still limp and stand even with an isolated fibular shaft fracture.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The common fibular nerve wraps around the neck of the fibula, making it vulnerable to compression causing 'foot drop'.

name: Radius
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of the lateral radius bone rotating gracefully around the ulna to turn the palm upward.
core_traits: One of the two long bones of the forearm, situated on the lateral (thumb) side
Features a unique disc-shaped head proximally that pivots against the capitulum of the humerus
Rotates around the stationary ulna during pronation (palm down) and supination (palm up)
Distal end forms the major joint surface articulating with wrist carpal bones

facts_and_myths.claim: The radius is the most commonly fractured long bone in the entire human body.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Falling onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH injury) transmits force that breaks the distal radius, commonly known as a Colles' fracture.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: You can find your radial pulse by pressing gently on the thumb side of your wrist just over the distal radius.

facts_and_myths.claim: During forearm twisting, both the radius and ulna cross over each other like scissors.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The ulna remains largely stationary; only the mobile radius pivots and crosses diagonally over the ulna.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The bone is named 'radius' because it rotates around the ulna like the spoke of a wheel.

name: Ulna
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical render of the medial ulna showing the hook-shaped olecranon process locking into the elbow hinge.
core_traits: Long bone located on the medial (pinky finger) side of the forearm parallel to the radius
Features a prominent hook-like wrench process at its top called the olecranon
Forms the main hinge joint of the elbow with the trochlea of the humerus
The olecranon forms the bony, pointed tip of the elbow easily felt under the skin

facts_and_myths.claim: The hard pointy tip of your elbow that rests on a table is part of the ulna bone.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The olecranon process of the proximal ulna forms the elbow point and prevents hyperextension by locking into the olecranon fossa.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In ancient Egypt and Rome, the length of the ulna from elbow to fingertip defined the classic unit of length: the cubit.

facts_and_myths.claim: The ulna is the primary forearm bone responsible for articulating with the wrist carpal bones.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The ulna is separated from wrist carpal bones by a fibrocartilaginous disc; the radius forms nearly all direct wrist articulation.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A 'nightstick fracture' is an isolated fracture of the ulnar shaft caused by raising an arm to block a blow.

name: Clavicle
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of the gentle S-curved clavicle collarbone bridging the sternum to the shoulder blade.
core_traits: Slender, horizontally positioned S-shaped long bone spanning the base of the neck
Connects the axial skeleton (manubrium of the sternum) to the appendicular skeleton (scapula)
Acts as a strut holding the shoulder joint away from the trunk to allow maximum arm mobility
Transmits mechanical physical impacts from the upper limb directly into the axial skeleton

facts_and_myths.claim: The clavicle is the very first bone to begin ossification in a developing human embryo.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It begins intramembranous ossification around the fifth to sixth week of gestation, yet is the last bone to finish fusing (around age 25).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word clavicle comes from the Latin 'clavicula', meaning 'little key', describing its rotary movement during shoulder abduction.

facts_and_myths.claim: A broken collarbone always requires invasive surgical screws and titanium plates to heal.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The vast majority of midshaft clavicle fractures heal exceptionally well with non-operative treatment in a simple arm sling.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The collarbone is one of the most frequently broken bones in cycling and contact sports.

name: Scapula
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical render of the triangular flat scapula bone gliding smoothly along the posterior rib cage.
core_traits: Large, flat, triangular bone located on the posterolateral aspect of the thoracic cage
Features a prominent posterior spine ending in the acromion process at the shoulder tip
Possesses the shallow glenoid cavity articulating with the humerus to form the shoulder joint
Floats dynamically over the rib cage cushioned by muscle, providing wide arm mobility

facts_and_myths.claim: The scapula is connected to the posterior rib cage purely by muscular attachments without a bony joint.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The 'scapulothoracic joint' is a physiological joint made of gliding muscle layers, allowing the shoulder blade to glide freely in all planes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word scapula comes from ancient Greek and Latin words for 'spade' or 'shovel', reflecting its flat digging tool shape.

facts_and_myths.claim: Winged scapula is a normal cosmetic posture trait with zero muscle weakness.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Scapular winging occurs when the long thoracic nerve is damaged, paralyzing the serratus anterior muscle and lifting the bone away from the ribs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Four rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis) all originate on the scapula.

name: Sternum
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical cutaway of the tie-shaped sternum anchoring costal cartilages right over the cardiac silhouette.
core_traits: Flat, elongated bone located vertically in the anterior midline of the chest
Shaped like an necktie or dagger composed of three fused parts: manubrium, body, and xiphoid process
Anchors the clavicles and the costal cartilages of the first seven pairs of true ribs
Protects the underlying heart, great vessels, and trachea from frontal chest trauma

facts_and_myths.claim: Performing chest compressions during CPR often cracks or breaks the patient's ribs or sternum.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Proper depth compressions (2 inches deep) frequently fracture elderly costal cartilages or ribs, an acceptable tradeoff to save a life.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Open-heart surgeries cut the sternum down the middle (median sternotomy) and wire it back together like a zipper.

facts_and_myths.claim: The xiphoid process at the bottom of the sternum is a solid bone present from birth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The xiphoid begins as a flexible triangle of hyaline cartilage, typically not fully ossifying into bone until around age 40.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is a distinct tactile ridge on the chest used by doctors to count ribs and locate heart valves.

name: Patella
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical cutaway of the triangular patella kneecap embedded within the quadriceps and patellar tendon.
core_traits: Thick, flat, triangular bone located at the anterior front of the knee joint
Largest sesamoid bone (a bone embedded entirely within a tendon) in the human body
Embedded within the quadriceps tendon continuing as the patellar ligament into the tibia
Increases the mechanical leverage of the quadriceps muscle by holding the tendon away from the joint axis

facts_and_myths.claim: Human babies are born without hard bony kneecaps.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Infant kneecaps are soft pieces of cartilage that do not fully ossify into solid bone until between ages 2 and 6.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Cartilage on the backside of the patella is the thickest articular cartilage in the entire body (up to 6 mm thick).

facts_and_myths.claim: The patella is anchored by direct bone-to-bone fused joints with the femur and tibia.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The patella floats within tendons; it articulates dynamically with the femoral trochlear groove but has zero bony fusion.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word patella is Latin for 'small shallow dish' or 'frying pan', describing its concave inner contour.

name: Joints
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 cutaway of a synovial joint showing cartilage-capped bones gliding smoothly in a glowing fluid capsule.
core_traits: Physical junctions where two or more bones meet in the skeletal system
Classified structurally into fibrous (immovable sutures), cartilaginous (semi-movable), and synovial (freely movable)
Synovial joints feature an articular capsule lined with synovial membrane producing lubricating fluid
Types of synovial joints include ball-and-socket, hinge, pivot, saddle, condyloid, and gliding

facts_and_myths.claim: Cracking your knuckles causes permanent joint arthritis in old age.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Knuckle cracking is caused by cavitation bubbles bursting in synovial fluid; physician Donald Unger cracked one hand for 60 years with zero arthritis.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dr. Donald Unger won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2009 for proving knuckle cracking does not cause arthritis.

facts_and_myths.claim: Synovial fluid inside healthy joints has a lower coefficient of friction than ice sliding on ice.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Articular cartilage combined with lubricin and hyaluronic acid produces a friction coefficient of 0.001, five times slicker than wet ice.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The shoulder joint is the most mobile joint in the human body, but consequently the easiest to dislocate.

name: Cartilage
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 microscopic perspective of glassy, glistening blue-white hyaline cartilage capping bone ends with resilient chondrocytes.
core_traits: Tough, flexible, semi-rigid connective tissue found throughout the human body
Contains chondrocyte cells embedded in an abundant gel-like collagen and proteoglycan extracellular matrix
Exists in three distinct types: hyaline (glassy joint caps), elastic (ear pinna, epiglottis), and fibrocartilage (knee meniscus)
Avascular (contains no blood vessels or nerves), relying on slow diffusion for nutrition

facts_and_myths.claim: Damaged articular joint cartilage heals very poorly and slowly compared to broken bone.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because cartilage lacks blood vessels, repair cells and nutrients cannot rush to the site, making cartilage tears notoriously chronic.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Your outer ear and the tip of your nose are shaped entirely by flexible cartilage rather than bone.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cartilage contains rich sensory pain nerves that hurt immediately whenever it gets rubbed.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cartilage is completely aneural (has no nerves); arthritis pain comes from the underlying exposed bone (subchondral bone) and inflamed joint capsule.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sharks and rays have complete skeletons made entirely of cartilage with zero true bone.

name: Ligaments
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of taut, glistening white ligament bands crossing the knee joint stabilizing the femur and tibia.
core_traits: Short bands of tough, flexible, fibrous dense regular connective tissue
Connect bone to bone across joints, reinforcing and stabilizing joint capsules
Composed predominantly of densely packed parallel bundles of type I collagen fibers
Limit the abnormal range of joint motion to prevent dislocations and hyper-extensions

facts_and_myths.claim: Ligaments connect muscle to bone, while tendons connect bone to bone.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The reverse is true: ligaments connect bone to bone, whereas tendons attach muscles to bones.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A useful mnemonic: 'Ligaments Link bones, Tendons Tie muscle to bone'.

facts_and_myths.claim: A severe tear of a ligament like the ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) rarely heals on its own.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because the ACL is bathed in synovial fluid and has poor blood supply, complete tears typically require surgical reconstruction.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When you sprain an ankle, you have stretched or torn a ligament (most commonly the anterior talofibular ligament).

name: Tendons
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical perspective of glistening silvery-white tendon fibers merging seamlessly from skeletal muscle into periosteum bone.
core_traits: Tough, inelastic bands of dense fibrous connective tissue connecting skeletal muscle to bone
Transmit the mechanical pulling force generated by contracting muscle fibers directly to the skeleton
Composed of parallel rows of collagen fibers capable of withstanding immense tensile strain
Surrounded in high-friction areas by protective synovial tendon sheaths

facts_and_myths.claim: The Achilles tendon at the back of the heel is the largest and strongest tendon in the human body.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It can withstand tensile loads exceeding 1,000 pounds (over 4 times body weight) during sprinting and jumping.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Named after the mythical Greek warrior Achilles, whose heel was his only mortal vulnerable spot.

facts_and_myths.claim: Tendons are highly elastic rubber bands that stretch to double their length during muscle contractions.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tendons are stiff with very low elasticity (stretching only 4 to 8 percent) to efficiently transfer mechanical muscle force without energy lag.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Golgi tendon organs are sensory receptors embedded in tendons that tell the brain how much tension is being applied to prevent tearing.

name: Skeletal Muscles
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 anatomical view of striated skeletal muscle bundles glowing with sliding actin and myosin filaments during contraction.
core_traits: Voluntary muscle tissue anchored to the skeleton via collagenous tendons
Over 600 distinct skeletal muscles make up approximately 40 percent of adult body mass
Features characteristic microscopic striations formed by repeating sarcomere units of actin and myosin
Controlled directly by somatic motor neurons via conscious neuromuscular impulses

facts_and_myths.claim: Muscles can only pull bones toward them; they can never actively push bones away.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Muscle fibers only generate force by contracting (shortening); they work in antagonistic pairs like biceps and triceps to reverse motion.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The stapedius muscle in the middle ear is the smallest skeletal muscle in the human body, measuring just over one millimeter.

facts_and_myths.claim: Muscle soreness the day after intense exercise (DOMS) is caused by trapped lactic acid in muscles.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lactic acid clears from muscle tissue within an hour after exercise; DOMS is caused by microscopic tears in muscle fibers and inflammation.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Shaking after heavy lifting happens because motor units fatigue and fire asynchronously.

name: Smooth Muscle
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 microscopic visualization of spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells contracting in rhythmic synchronized peristaltic waves.
core_traits: Involuntary, non-striated muscle tissue found in the walls of hollow internal organs
Lines the gastrointestinal tract, blood vessels, airways, bladder, and uterus
Composed of spindle-shaped mononucleated cells lacking organized sarcomere bands
Governed automatically by the autonomic nervous system, hormones, and local stretch reflexes

facts_and_myths.claim: Smooth muscle can sustain prolonged tonic contractions for hours with remarkably little energy consumption.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Using the 'latch-state' mechanism, smooth muscle maintains blood vessel tone and organ sphincters using a fraction of ATP that skeletal muscle requires.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The arrector pili muscles that raise your body hairs to cause goosebumps are made of smooth muscle.

facts_and_myths.claim: Humans can consciously flex and control their internal smooth muscle on demand.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Smooth muscle operates completely below conscious cognitive awareness, regulated by autonomic nerves and physiological hormones.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: During childbirth, smooth muscle in the myometrium of the uterus produces the strongest muscular contractions in the human body.

name: Cardiac Muscle
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 microscopic rendering of branched cardiac myocytes interconnected by glowing intercalated discs pulsing in continuous unison.
core_traits: Specialized involuntary striated muscle tissue found exclusively within the walls of the heart
Cells (cardiomyocytes) are branched and interconnected by intercalated discs containing gap junctions
Packs immense concentrations of mitochondria, generating ATP almost purely through aerobic metabolism
Possesses intrinsic autorhythmicity, contracting tirelessly without fatigue roughly 100,000 times a day

facts_and_myths.claim: Cardiac muscle cells contain so many mitochondria that they occupy up to 40 percent of the cell volume.
facts_and_myths.explanation: This massive mitochondrial density ensures the heart never suffers muscle fatigue under normal oxygenated conditions.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: If isolated cardiac muscle cells are placed next to each other in a petri dish, they will begin beating in perfect synchronization.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cardiac muscle easily regenerates new healthy muscle cells after an ischemic heart attack.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Adult cardiomyocytes have very limited regenerative ability; dead heart muscle is permanently replaced by stiff fibrous scar tissue.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Intercalated discs allow electrical ions to flow instantly between cells, making the heart contract as a single functional syncytium.

name: Biceps
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of the two-headed biceps brachii flexing on the anterior upper arm turning the palm upward.
core_traits: Two-headed skeletal muscle situated on the anterior compartment of the upper arm
Originates from the scapula with two distinct heads: the long head and the short head
Inserts onto the radial tuberosity of the forearm radius bone
Primary supine rotator of the forearm and powerful flexor of the elbow joint

facts_and_myths.claim: The biceps brachii is the most powerful supinator of the forearm (turning the palm upward).
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because it inserts on the radius, the biceps acts like a cord wrapped around an axle, powerfully twisting the forearm to turn keys or screwdrivers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The name 'biceps' comes from Latin meaning 'two-headed', referring to its dual scapular attachments.

facts_and_myths.claim: The biceps is the primary muscle responsible for lifting the elbow from a straight position.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The underlying brachialis muscle is the primary workhorse flexor of the elbow; the biceps aids flexion mainly when the palm is turned up.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A 'Popeye muscle deformity' occurs when the tendon of the long head of the biceps ruptures, bunching the muscle into a ball.

name: Triceps
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical render of the horseshoe-shaped three-headed triceps extending the elbow on the back of the upper arm.
core_traits: Three-headed skeletal muscle located on the posterior compartment of the upper arm
Composed of three distinct heads: long head, lateral head, and medial head
Inserts via a broad tendon onto the olecranon process of the ulna at the elbow tip
Primary extensor muscle of the elbow joint, working antagonistically against the biceps

facts_and_myths.claim: The triceps accounts for roughly 60 percent of the total muscle mass of the upper arm.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Despite the cultural popularity of biceps, the triceps is significantly larger in cross-sectional volume and mass.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Every time you perform a push-up or bench press, your triceps provide the extension power to lock out the elbows.

facts_and_myths.claim: The triceps muscle can actively flex the elbow inward toward the chest.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The triceps exclusively extends (straightens) the elbow; it is physically impossible for it to flex the joint.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The long head of the triceps is unique because it crosses the shoulder joint, helping to stabilize and adduct the arm.

name: Quadriceps
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of the powerful four-part quadriceps muscle spanning the front thigh to straighten the knee.
core_traits: Large group of four skeletal muscles located on the anterior compartment of the thigh
Consists of rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius
Crucial extensor of the knee joint, essential for walking, running, jumping, and squatting
Converges into the common quadriceps tendon encapsulating the patella kneecap

facts_and_myths.claim: The quadriceps muscle group contains the strongest and most voluminous muscle mass in the human body.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Together, the four heads of the quadriceps generate massive force capable of supporting full-body locomotion and heavy lifting.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The rectus femoris is the only head of the quad that crosses both the hip and knee joints, flexing the hip and extending the knee.

facts_and_myths.claim: Quadriceps muscles are responsible for pulling the heel backward toward the glutes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Bending the knee backward is performed by the opposing posterior hamstring muscles; the quads forcefully straighten the knee.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The 'teardrop muscle' above the inside of the knee is the vastus medialis oblique (VMO).

name: Hamstrings
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical perspective of the three hamstring muscles coursing down the posterior thigh to bend the knee.
core_traits: Group of three skeletal muscles located on the posterior compartment of the thigh
Composed of the biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus
Originates primarily from the ischial tuberosity (the sit bone) of the pelvis
Functions antagonistically to the quadriceps: flexes the knee joint and extends the hip

facts_and_myths.claim: Hamstring strains are among the most common and recurrent injuries in sprinting sports.
facts_and_myths.explanation: During terminal swing phase in sprinting, the hamstrings undergo rapid eccentric elongation under heavy load, making them prone to tears.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The term 'hamstring' comes from butchers hanging slaughtered pig carcasses (hams) by the strong tendons behind the knee.

facts_and_myths.claim: Hamstring muscles only cross and act upon a single joint (the knee).
facts_and_myths.explanation: All three hamstrings (except the short head of biceps femoris) are biarticular, crossing both the hip and knee joints.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tight hamstrings pull downward on the pelvis, flattening the lumbar spine and contributing to chronic lower back pain.

name: Abdominal Muscles
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical render of layered abdominal muscles showing the segmented six-pack rectus abdominis and crossing obliques.
core_traits: Layered muscular wall supporting and encasing the anterior and lateral abdomen
Composed of rectus abdominis, external obliques, internal obliques, and transversus abdominis
Stabilizes the lumbar spine and pelvis, maintains upright posture, and facilitates trunk flexion
Assists in breathing, coughing, vomiting, and raising intra-abdominal pressure during exertion

facts_and_myths.claim: Doing thousands of abdominal crunches burns belly fat selectively off your waistline.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Spot reduction is a biological myth; fat loss occurs systemically across the whole body when a caloric deficit is achieved.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The 'six-pack' appearance is created by fibrous connective bands called tendinous intersections crossing the rectus abdominis.

facts_and_myths.claim: The deepest abdominal muscle, transversus abdominis, acts like a natural internal corset.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Its horizontal fibers wrap around the midsection, compressing abdominal contents and providing crucial stabilization for the lower spine.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The linea alba is the fibrous white seam running vertically down the midline between left and right abdominal muscles.

name: Gluteus Maximus
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical visual of the massive gluteus maximus anchoring the pelvis and extending the femur for upright posture.
core_traits: Largest, heaviest, and most powerful individual skeletal muscle in the entire human body
Forms the bulk of the fleshy buttock contour on each side of the posterior pelvis
Powerful extensor of the hip joint, driving human bipedal running, sprinting, and climbing stairs
Crucial evolutionary adaptation enabling sustained upright bipedal human locomotion

facts_and_myths.claim: Humans evolved an exceptionally massive gluteus maximus specifically for endurance running.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Unlike chimps, humans have an enlarged gluteus maximus that prevents the torso from pitching forward during upright running.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: While standing quietly, the gluteus maximus is largely relaxed; it activates strongly when climbing stairs or sprinting.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sitting directly on your buttocks for prolonged hours exercises and strengthens the gluteus maximus.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Prolonged sitting compresses and deactivates the muscle, causing gluteal amnesia and hip flexor tightness.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The gluteus maximus is frequently used as a safe site for deep intramuscular medical injections.

name: Achilles Tendon
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of the thick cord-like Achilles tendon connecting calf muscles into the calcaneus heel bone.
core_traits: Thickest and strongest tendon in the entire human musculoskeletal system
Connects the gastrocnemius and soleus calf muscles to the calcaneus (heel bone)
Stores and releases elastic energy like a spring with every running step, reducing metabolic energy cost
Subject to sudden traumatic rupture producing an audible pop like a gunshot

facts_and_myths.claim: When an Achilles tendon snaps, people frequently believe they were kicked violently from behind.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The sudden release of high elastic tension feels so violent and abrupt that patients turn around expecting to see an attacker.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Human Achilles tendons store and return about 35 percent of the energy needed for running strides.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Achilles tendon receives abundant blood flow across its entire length, allowing rapid healing.
facts_and_myths.explanation: There is an avascular zone 2 to 6 centimeters above the heel with poor blood supply, which is where most ruptures occur.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Thompson test diagnoses a torn Achilles: squeezing the calf fails to flex the foot downward.

name: Epidermis
visual_anchor: Microscopic vertical 9:16 cross-section of the stratified squamous epidermis with keratinized surface flakes glowing in polarized light.
core_traits: Outermost epithelial layer of the skin providing an impermeable physical and biological barrier
Avascular layer composed primarily of keratinocytes, with melanocytes, Langerhans, and Merkel cells
Divided into five distinct cellular strata, topped by the dead cornified stratum corneum
Continually renews itself from the basal layer, shedding roughly 40,000 dead cells every minute

facts_and_myths.claim: The outermost layer of your skin that touches the world is composed entirely of dead cells.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The stratum corneum is composed of dead, flattened keratinocytes packed with tough waterproof keratin protein.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Your entire epidermis replaces itself completely every 4 to 6 weeks.

facts_and_myths.claim: A paper cut bleeds profusely because the epidermis is packed with dense blood vessels.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The epidermis contains zero blood vessels; if a paper cut bleeds, it has penetrated into the vascular dermis below.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The thickest epidermis on the body is on the palms and soles (up to 1.5 mm), featuring an extra layer called stratum lucidum.

name: Hair Follicles
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 microscopic cutaway of a bulbous hair follicle rooted deep in the dermis sprouting an illuminated keratin shaft.
core_traits: Tunnel-shaped mini-organs embedded in the dermal skin layer that produce hair strands
Contain rapidly dividing matrix stem cells nourished by a vascular dermal papilla at the base
Associated with a sebaceous oil gland and an involuntary arrector pili smooth muscle
Cycle continuously through three distinct growth phases: anagen (growth), catagen (transition), and telogen (rest)

facts_and_myths.claim: Plucking one gray hair causes two or three gray hairs to grow back in its place.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Each follicle can only grow a single hair shaft; plucking does not affect neighboring follicles, which gray at their own genetic pace.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hair follicle matrix cells are among the fastest dividing cells in the body, which is why chemotherapy causes hair loss.

facts_and_myths.claim: Hair follicle cells are completely dead once the hair shaft emerges above the skin surface.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The hair shaft is dead polymerized keratin; only the root bulb inside the follicle beneath the scalp is alive.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Humans have roughly 5 million hair follicles across the body, approximately the same density as chimpanzees.

name: Sweat Glands
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of coiled tubular sweat glands in the dermis expelling clear droplet perspiration through skin pores.
core_traits: Coiled tubular exocrine glands distributed throughout human skin producing perspiration
Two main varieties: eccrine glands (thermoregulation worldwide) and apocrine glands (armpits and groin)
An average human possesses between 2 to 4 million sweat glands across the body
Secretes hypotonic watery fluid that evaporates from the skin to dissipate excess body heat

facts_and_myths.claim: Freshly secreted human sweat is completely odorless until broken down by skin bacteria.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sweat itself is sterile and odorless; body odor occurs when surface skin bacteria metabolize apocrine fats and proteins into thioalcohols.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The highest density of eccrine sweat glands is located on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sweating heavily in a sauna flushes dangerous chemical toxins and heavy metals from your organs.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sweat is 99 percent water with trace minerals; the liver and kidneys perform virtually 100 percent of body detoxification.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Humans can produce up to 2 to 3 liters of sweat per hour during intense athletic exercise in extreme heat.

name: Fingernails
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 macro perspective of a translucent curved fingernail rooted in the nail matrix with the white lunula crescent visible.
core_traits: Hard protective plates of translucent keratin covering the dorsal tips of fingers and toes
Produced by living germinal matrix cells tucked beneath the proximal nail fold (cuticle)
Features a visible whitish crescent moon shape near the base called the lunula
Enhances fingertip tactile discrimination and assists in grasping and manipulating tiny objects

facts_and_myths.claim: Human fingernails continue growing for several days after a person dies.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Nails do not grow after death; postmortem dehydration shrinks surrounding skin and cuticles, creating the optical illusion of longer nails.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fingernails grow roughly 3 to 4 times faster than toenails, averaging about 3 millimeters per month.

facts_and_myths.claim: White spots on fingernails (leukonychia) are caused by a serious calcium deficiency in your diet.
facts_and_myths.explanation: White spots are almost always caused by minor micro-trauma to the nail matrix (like bumping your finger), not lack of calcium.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Nails on your dominant hand generally grow faster because increased blood flow and micro-use stimulate matrix activity.

name: Sebaceous Glands
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 microscopic cutaway showing a lobed sebaceous gland secreting golden lubricating sebum into a hair follicle canal.
core_traits: Microscopic exocrine glands located in the skin that secrete an oily or waxy substance called sebum
Usually connected directly to hair follicles, discharging sebum through the follicular canal
Abundant on the face, scalp, and upper back, but completely absent from the palms and soles
Sebum waterproofs and lubricates skin and hair while inhibiting bacterial and fungal proliferation

facts_and_myths.claim: Acne develops when excess sebum mixes with dead skin cells and bacteria inside the pore.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Overactive sebaceous glands plug pores, creating an anaerobic environment where Cutibacterium acnes bacteria proliferate.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sebaceous glands are holocrine glands: their cells disintegrate entirely to release their oily contents.

facts_and_myths.claim: Eating greasy chocolate and french fries causes immediate excess sebum secretion and pimples.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dietary oils do not travel directly to skin oil glands; hormones (androgens) drive sebum production, though high-glycemic foods can influence hormones.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Newborn babies are born covered in vernix caseosa, a protective white cheese-like coating made by fetal sebaceous glands.

name: Tooth Enamel
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 macro perspective of sparkling translucent tooth enamel crystals resisting mechanical grinding pressures.
core_traits: Thin, hard outer shell covering the anatomical crown of human teeth
Hardest and most highly mineralized biological substance in the human body
Composed of 96 percent crystalline hydroxyapatite minerals and 4 percent water and organic matrix
Contains no living cells or blood vessels, making it completely unable to biologically regenerate once lost

facts_and_myths.claim: Acidic soda drinks can dissolve and erode tooth enamel without bacteria even being present.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Acids with pH below 5.5 chemically demineralize crystalline hydroxyapatite directly, stripping away enamel enamel prisms.
