facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Enamel can remineralize slightly using calcium, phosphate, and fluoride from saliva, but it cannot regrow lost layers.

facts_and_myths.claim: Brushing your teeth violently with stiff bristles makes tooth enamel grow back thicker.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Abrasive, vigorous brushing physically scrubs away enamel (abrasion), exposing yellowish sensitive dentin underneath.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tooth enamel is semi-translucent; the yellowish color of healthy teeth comes from the underlying dentin showing through.

name: Sense of Sight
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 visualization of rainbow light beams entering the iris and mapping into kaleidoscopic neuronal signals in the visual cortex.
core_traits: Special sensory modality that translates visible electromagnetic light wavelengths into mental images
Processed through the optical apparatus (cornea, lens) onto the neurosensory retina
Accounts for roughly 80 percent of all sensory information processed by the human brain
Primary visual processing occurs in the visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) in the occipital lobe

facts_and_myths.claim: The human eye actually projects upside-down images onto the retina, which the brain flips right-side up.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Optics of convex lenses invert incoming light rays; the visual cortex inverts the sensory neural data so we perceive reality upright.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Psychologist George Stratton wore image-inverting prism goggles for eight days; by day five, his brain adapted and saw the world upright again.

facts_and_myths.claim: Humans can see UV light and infrared light just as clearly as honeybees and snakes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Human vision is strictly limited to visible spectrum wavelengths between roughly 380 and 740 nanometers; the lens filters out UV rays.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: People who have their lenses removed (aphakia) can actually perceive near-ultraviolet light as pale whitish-violet.

name: Sense of Hearing
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 visualization of undulating sound waves flowing into the ear canal, activating auditory hair cells in the temporal lobe.
core_traits: Sensory modality capable of perceiving mechanical pressure vibrations propagating through air or water
Normal human hearing spans a frequency range from roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz
Operates through acoustic sound capture (pinna), mechanical amplification (ossicles), and neural transduction (cochlea)
Processed bilaterally in the primary auditory cortex within the superior temporal gyrus

facts_and_myths.claim: The ability to hear high-pitched acoustic frequencies naturally diminishes as humans age (presbycusis).
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cochlear hair cells at the basal entrance that register high pitches sustain the most wear over a lifetime and die off first.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Teenagers can hear the 17.4 kHz 'Mosquito ringtone', whereas most adults over age 25 cannot detect it.

facts_and_myths.claim: When you sleep peacefully, your ears shut down completely and stop transducing sound waves.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Ears transduce sound 24/7; during sleep, the thalamus acts as a sensory gatekeeper, filtering out non-threatening background sounds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hearing is considered by hospice physicians to be the very last sensory perception lost before death.

name: Sense of Smell
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 visualization of airborne scent molecules entering the nasal cavity and binding to glowing olfactory receptors directly sparking limbic memories.
core_traits: Chemical sensory modality that detects airborne volatile chemical compounds (odorants)
Mediated by roughly 400 distinct functional olfactory receptor gene families in the nasal epithelium
Transmits signals directly to the olfactory bulb and limbic system without prior thalamic gating
Responsible for the overwhelming majority of nuanced flavor perception during eating

facts_and_myths.claim: Humans can smell the fresh scent of rainfall on dry soil (petrichor) at fractions of parts per billion.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Human noses are exquisitely sensitive to geosmin, a bacterial metabolite released when rain hits dry earth, beating shark blood sensitivity.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Smell receptors can regenerate throughout adult life from basal stem cells every 30 to 60 days.

facts_and_myths.claim: Holding your nose while eating food only alters your breathing and leaves taste completely unaffected.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pinching your nose eliminates retronasal olfaction, making apples and onions taste virtually identical as sweet-watery crunch.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Anosmia is the complete loss of the sense of smell, famously brought to public attention as a symptom of COVID-19.

name: Sense of Taste
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 cutaway of taste buds on tongue papillae firing neural flavor cascades into the gustatory insular cortex.
core_traits: Chemical sensory system detecting soluble chemicals dissolved in saliva inside the mouth
Distinguishes five verified basic taste qualities: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami
Evolved to guide caloric nutrition (sweet, umami) while warning against toxic poisons (bitter, sour)
Innervated by cranial nerves VII (facial), IX (glossopharyngeal), and X (vagus)

facts_and_myths.claim: Humans are biologically born with an instinctive innate revulsion toward bitter tastes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because most natural plant toxins and poisons are bitter alkaloids, human infants possess an evolutionary hardwired disgust reflex to bitterness.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Miracle fruit (Synsepalum dulcificum) contains miraculin, which temporarily binds taste receptors and turns sour lemons sweet.

facts_and_myths.claim: Everyone perceives tastes with identical intensity and sensitivity across foods.
facts_and_myths.explanation: 'Supertasters' have high fungiform papillae density and TAS2R38 gene variants, tasting bitterness in broccoli and coffee with extreme intensity.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Umami, the savory taste of monosodium glutamate and aged parmesan cheese, was identified in 1908 by Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda.

name: Sense of Touch
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of skin mechanoreceptors (Meissner, Pacinian, Merkel) firing glowing neural pulses as a fingertip brushes silk.
core_traits: Sensory modality encompassing pressure, vibration, texture, temperature, and pain across the skin
Mediated by specialized mechanoreceptors: Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner's corpuscles, Merkel discs, and Ruffini endings
Mapped across the primary somatosensory cortex along the famous cortical sensory homunculus
Fingertips, lips, tongue, and hands have the highest tactile receptor density and brain representation

facts_and_myths.claim: You cannot tickle yourself because your cerebellum predicts the sensory consequence of your own movements.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The cerebellum sends an efference copy predicting the tactile stimulus, canceling out the surprising sensory tickle response.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The sensory homunculus in the parietal cortex depicts humans with enormous hands and giant lips reflecting receptor density.

facts_and_myths.claim: Skin tactile receptors are spaced uniformly across every square centimeter of the human body.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fingertips have a two-point discrimination threshold under 2 millimeters, whereas the back requires points to be 40 millimeters apart to tell them apart.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pacinian corpuscles deep in the dermis detect high-frequency vibrations up to 1,000 Hz, such as running a finger over rough fabric.

name: Sense of Balance
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 graphic of a tightrope walker with internal vestibular inner ear canals and cerebellar balancing networks glowing golden.
core_traits: Sensory perception governing physical equilibrium, gravitational orientation, and directional acceleration
Orchestrated primarily by the vestibular apparatus of the inner ear (semicircular canals and otolith organs)
Integrates visual input, inner ear fluid dynamics, and proprioceptive joint sensors in the brainstem and cerebellum
Controls the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR), keeping vision steady when your head bobs while running

facts_and_myths.claim: The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) moves your eyes in the exact opposite direction of head movement to keep vision stable.
facts_and_myths.explanation: If you shake your head 'no' while reading text, the text stays crystal clear because VOR adjusts eye muscles within 10 milliseconds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Motion sickness occurs when sensory inputs conflict - such as your eyes seeing a stationary car cabin while your inner ear feels acceleration.

facts_and_myths.claim: Inner ear fluid is the only sensory input the brain uses to maintain balance.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Balance is a triad: vestibular signals, visual cues, and proprioception from leg joints; you need at least two working to stay upright easily.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Otolith organs (utricle and saccule) use tiny microscopic stones of calcium carbonate that slide over hair cells under gravity.

name: Proprioception
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical render of glowing muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs sensing joint angles in the dark without vision.
core_traits: The body's intrinsic sense of its own position, movement, and posture in space without using vision
Mediated by specialized mechanoreceptors: muscle spindles (stretch), Golgi tendon organs (tension), and joint capsule receptors
Allows you to touch your index finger to your nose with eyes closed or navigate stairs in pitch darkness
Processed subconsciously in the cerebellum and consciously in the primary somatosensory cortex

facts_and_myths.claim: Police officers use proprioception tests (touching your nose with eyes closed) to check for alcohol intoxication.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Alcohol severely disrupts cerebellar coordination and proprioceptive feedback loops, making smooth closed-eye motor targeting impossible.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ian Waterman completely lost his sense of touch and proprioception from a viral infection and had to learn to walk purely using visual guidance.

facts_and_myths.claim: Proprioception is identical to the vestibular balance sense located inside the inner ear.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Vestibular sense detects head tilt and acceleration via inner ear fluid; proprioception senses limb position and muscle stretch throughout the body.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Phantom limb sensations occur when cortical proprioceptive maps remain active after a limb has been amputated.

name: Pain Perception
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of unmyelinated nociceptive nerve fibers flashing electric crimson warnings from a skin cut up to the cerebral cortex.
core_traits: Sensory and emotional experience triggered by actual or potential tissue damage
Initiated by specialized sensory receptors called nociceptors sensitive to heat, cold, mechanical pressure, or chemical irritants
Transmitted via fast A-delta fibers (sharp, localized pain) and slow unmyelinated C fibers (dull, throbbing ache)
Modulated in the spinal cord and brainstem by descending endorphin and enkephalin analgesic pathways

facts_and_myths.claim: People born with congenital insensitivity to pain (CIP) live longer because they never suffer physical pain.
facts_and_myths.explanation: CIP is life-threatening; without warning pain, sufferers frequently bite through their tongues, burn themselves, and ignore broken bones or burst appendices.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Redheads often have MC1R gene mutations that make them require approximately 20 percent more general anesthesia to suppress pain.

facts_and_myths.claim: Referred pain happens because visceral organs share spinal cord pathways with superficial skin areas.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A heart attack causes left arm and jaw pain because sensory signals from the heart converge onto the same spinal segments as arm dermatomes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The brain tissue itself has zero nociceptors and feels no pain, which allows awake brain surgery.

name: Heartbeat
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 visualization of the muscular heart contracting in rhythmic lub-dub cycles with glowing electrical sinoatrial waves.
core_traits: Rhythmic contraction and relaxation cycle of the heart muscle pumping blood throughout the body
Normal resting adult heartbeat ranges between 60 and 100 beats per minute (bpm)
Initiated intrinsically by electrical action potentials originating in the sinoatrial (SA) node pacemaker
Consists of two phases: ventricular systole (pumping contraction) and ventricular diastole (filling relaxation)

facts_and_myths.claim: The iconic 'lub-dub' acoustic sound of a heartbeat is made by the heart valves snapping shut.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The first sound (lub/S1) is the closure of mitral and tricuspid valves; the second sound (dub/S2) is aortic and pulmonary valve closure.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over an average 80-year human lifespan, the heart beats more than 3 billion times without ever taking a vacation.

facts_and_myths.claim: The heart stops beating completely for a fraction of a second every single time you sneeze.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sneezing changes intrathoracic pressure and may momentarily alter rhythm or delay a beat, but the heart never stops entirely.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Elite endurance athletes can develop a resting heart rate below 35 bpm (athletic bradycardia) due to high stroke volume.

name: Pulse
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of two fingers gently palpating the radial pulse on the thumb-side wrist with rhythmic ripple shockwaves.
core_traits: Rhythmic tactile shockwave felt over superficial arteries generated by left ventricular ejection
Common palpation points include the radial artery (wrist), carotid artery (neck), and femoral artery (groin)
Directly reflects heart rate, cardiac rhythm regularity, and arterial wall elasticity
Propagates along arterial walls faster than the actual physical liquid speed of blood flow

facts_and_myths.claim: The pulse wave travels through arterial walls roughly 10 times faster than the physical blood cells flowing inside.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The pulse is a mechanical pressure shockwave travelling through elastic vessel walls at 5 to 10 m/s, whereas blood flows at only 0.5 m/s.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: You should never check someone's pulse using your thumb because your thumb's own strong radial artery can trick you.

facts_and_myths.claim: A person's resting pulse rate is completely fixed and never fluctuates during ordinary daily life.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pulse changes dynamically every minute in response to caffeine, emotional stress, ambient temperature, posture, and hydration.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When you inhale, pulse naturally speeds up slightly, and when you exhale, it slows down (respiratory sinus arrhythmia).

name: Blood Pressure
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 medical visual of a sphygmomanometer mercury column displaying 120 over 80 mmHg beside pulsating arterial walls.
core_traits: Lateral hydrostatic pressure exerted by circulating blood against the walls of systemic arteries
Expressed as two numbers: systolic pressure (peak during heart contraction) over diastolic pressure (minimum at rest)
Standard normal healthy resting blood pressure in an adult is considered around 120/80 mmHg
Regulated by the autonomic baroreceptor reflex and the hormonal renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)

facts_and_myths.claim: High blood pressure (hypertension) is famously called the 'silent killer' because it usually produces zero symptoms.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Millions live with dangerously elevated blood pressure without headaches or dizziness until it triggers a sudden heart attack or stroke.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Giraffes have blood pressure roughly double that of humans (around 280/180 mmHg) to pump blood 8 feet straight up to their brains.

facts_and_myths.claim: Drinking a glass of water instantly reduces severe hypertension back to baseline permanently.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Water hydration does not cure hypertension; managing blood pressure requires reduced sodium, exercise, medication, and dietary control.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: 'White coat hypertension' is when a patient's blood pressure spikes artificially just from anxiety in a doctor's clinic.

name: Breathing
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 visual of glowing oxygen air streams entering the nasal passages down expanding bronchial lungs in rhythmic breath.
core_traits: Physiological process of inhaling oxygen-rich air into lungs and exhaling carbon dioxide waste
Adults take approximately 12 to 20 breaths per minute at rest, totaling roughly 20,000 breaths per day
Inspiration is an active muscular process driven by diaphragm and external intercostal contraction
Regulated automatically by respiratory centers in the medulla oblongata sensing arterial CO2 and pH

facts_and_myths.claim: The biological urge to breathe is driven primarily by excess carbon dioxide buildup rather than lack of oxygen.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Central chemoreceptors in the brainstem detect acidifying drops in blood pH caused by rising CO2 levels, forcing you to gasp.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hyperventilating drops CO2 without adding oxygen, which can cause shallow-water blackout in swimmers.

facts_and_myths.claim: Humans breathe through both nostrils equally and identically at all times of day.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Through the nasal cycle, the autonomic system swells erectile tissue in one nostril at a time, switching dominant airflow every 2 to 4 hours.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: You exhale roughly half a liter of water vapor every day just through ordinary respiration.

name: Digestion
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 full gastrointestinal cutaway following glowing food breaking down mechanically and chemically from mouth to colon.
core_traits: Complex physiological breakdown of large ingested food molecules into absorbable microscopic nutrients
Combines mechanical breakdown (chewing, stomach churning) and chemical enzymatic hydrolysis
Involves the sequential GI tract: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine
Aided by accessory organs including salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, and pancreas

facts_and_myths.claim: Swallowed chewing gum takes seven full years to digest inside the human stomach.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While synthetic gum base cannot be digested by enzymes, it moves through the intestines and passes harmlessly within days.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The rumbling stomach sound you hear when hungry is called borborygmi, caused by peristaltic waves squeezing gas and fluid.

facts_and_myths.claim: The total journey of food through the complete human digestive system typically takes 24 to 72 hours.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Food spends roughly 2 to 5 hours in the stomach, 2 to 6 hours in the small intestine, and 10 to 59 hours in the colon.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Roughly 90 percent of the human body's total serotonin is manufactured inside the digestive tract by gut enterochromaffin cells.

name: Reflexes
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 diagram of the patellar tendon tap: sensory signal shooting into spinal cord and immediately kicking the lower leg forward.
core_traits: Involuntary, instantaneous motor responses to sensory stimuli executed without conscious brain deliberation
Routed through a neural pathway known as a reflex arc: sensor, sensory neuron, spinal interneuron, motor neuron, muscle
Protects the body from injury through rapid actions like the withdrawal reflex from hot objects
Common clinical examples include the patellar knee-jerk reflex, pupillary light reflex, and corneal blink reflex

facts_and_myths.claim: The patellar knee-jerk reflex arc contains only two neurons and zero brain involvement.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A monosynaptic reflex: the sensory neuron directly synapses onto the motor neuron in the lumbar spinal cord, firing within 20 milliseconds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Babinski reflex is normal in infants (toes fan out) but indicates upper motor neuron brain damage if present in adults.

facts_and_myths.claim: Reflexes can be trained through willpower to disappear completely in a single afternoon.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Primitive spinal reflexes are hardwired evolutionary survival circuits; they cannot be erased through conscious willpower alone.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The grasp reflex in human newborn babies is strong enough that an infant can support its own body weight hanging from a bar.

name: Yawning
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 expressive visual of a wide open mouth yawn stretching jaw muscles with cool airflow circulating to the brain.
core_traits: Involuntary reflex consisting of a deep inhalation with wide jaw stretching followed by slow exhalation
Universal physiological behavior found across virtually all vertebrate animals
Triggers include fatigue, sleep transitions, boredom, stress, and seeing or hearing another person yawn
Primary physiological hypothesis suggests it functions to cool the brain and promote cortical arousal

facts_and_myths.claim: Yawning is psychologically contagious among humans, chimpanzees, and domesticated dogs.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Contagious yawning activates mirror neuron systems and empathy networks in the brain; people with higher empathy yawn more in response.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Human fetuses begin yawning inside the womb as early as the eleventh week of gestation.

facts_and_myths.claim: Yawning is the body's emergency method to replenish dangerously depleted blood oxygen levels.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Studies giving people pure oxygen showed zero change in yawning frequency; the oxygen theory was debunked decades ago.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pandiculation is the medical term for the pleasurable combination of yawning and full-body muscular stretching.

name: Hiccups
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical view of sudden diaphragm twitch spasm abruptly snapping the vocal cords shut with acoustic 'hic' sound waves.
core_traits: Sudden, involuntary spasmodic contraction of the muscular diaphragm and intercostal muscles
Immediately followed by an abrupt snapping closure of the vocal cords (glottis), generating the signature 'hic' sound
Triggered by eating too quickly, carbonated sodas, spicy foods, sudden temperature shifts, or excitement
Medical term is singultus, derived from the Latin word for 'sobbing' or 'catching one's breath'

facts_and_myths.claim: Drinking a glass of cold water while holding your breath can effectively cure acute hiccups.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Swallowing stimulates the vagus nerve while breath-holding raises CO2 levels, both helping reset the spasmodic phrenic nerve reflex arc.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Charles Osborne of Iowa holds the Guinness World Record for hiccuping non-stop for 68 years (1922-1990).

facts_and_myths.claim: Hiccups are an indicator that a teenager's physical height is experiencing a sudden growth spurt.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hiccups are purely mechanical spasms of the phrenic nerve and diaphragm; they have zero correlation with skeletal growth spurts.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many evolutionary biologists believe hiccups are an ancient remnant of amphibian gill ventilation reflexes.

name: Sneezing
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 high-speed photography render of an explosive sneeze blasting thousands of microscopic aerosol droplets from mouth and nose.
core_traits: Semi-autonomous convulsive expulsion of air from the lungs through the nose and mouth
Protective reflex triggered by irritation of the nasal respiratory mucous membranes
Orchestrated by the sneeze center located in the medulla oblongata via the trigeminal nerve
Expels irritating foreign particles, dust, pollen, and excess mucus at high velocity

facts_and_myths.claim: Looking directly at bright sunlight can cause roughly one in four people to suddenly sneeze.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Known as the photic sneeze reflex (ACHOO syndrome), optic nerve stimulation crosses over into the nearby trigeminal nerve.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sneeze droplets can travel out of the mouth at speeds up to 100 miles per hour and spread droplets up to 20 feet.

facts_and_myths.claim: If you sneeze with your eyes open, your eyeballs will physically pop out of their sockets.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The blink reflex during sneezing is an involuntary brainstem reflex; extraocular muscles hold eyeballs firmly in place regardless.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It is biologically impossible to sneeze while in deep REM sleep because motor neurons are actively inhibited.

name: Coughing
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 anatomical visual of sudden deep inspiration, glottis closure, and explosive airway clearing blast out of the trachea.
core_traits: Vital protective airway reflex that forcefully clears the trachea, bronchi, and lungs of foreign irritants and mucus
Consists of three sequential phases: deep inhalation, glottis closure with thoracic pressure buildup, and explosive release
Triggered by mechanical or chemical stimulation of cough receptors along the respiratory tract
Transmitted through the vagus nerve (CN X) to the cough center in the medulla oblongata

facts_and_myths.claim: An explosive cough can propel air out of the human respiratory tract at speeds up to 50 miles per hour.
facts_and_myths.explanation: High intrathoracic pressures generated against the closed glottis release air velocities of 50 to 60 mph, clearing mucus plugs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Chronic coughing can generate enough violent muscular force to fracture lower ribs in elderly or osteoporotic individuals.

facts_and_myths.claim: Suppressing every single cough with over-the-counter medication is the best way to speed up pneumonia recovery.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Productive coughing is a vital immune mechanism that evacuates infective bacterial sputum; suppressing it can worsen lung infections.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The cough reflex can be triggered voluntarily from the cerebral cortex, unlike the largely involuntary sneeze reflex.

name: Blinking
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 macro perspective of human eyelids sweeping downward in a fraction of a second spreading a glistening tear film.
core_traits: Rapid semi-involuntary closing and reopening of the eyelids
Spreads tear film uniformly across the cornea, removing dust, maintaining optical clarity, and preventing desiccation
Humans blink approximately 15 to 20 times per minute, totaling roughly 14,000 to 20,000 blinks daily
Controlled by the orbicularis oculi (closure, CN VII) and levator palpebrae superioris (opening, CN III)

facts_and_myths.claim: A single blink takes only about 100 to 150 milliseconds to complete.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Blinking is so fast that the human brain suppresses visual awareness during the eyelid closure, preventing you from noticing the momentary blackness.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When reading books or staring at smartphone and computer screens, human blink rates drop by up to 60 percent, causing dry eyes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Blinking occurs only in response to conscious irritation or foreign dust striking the eyelashes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Spontaneous blinking is driven by a dopamine-regulated central neural pacemaker in the brainstem, occurring constantly without any external stimulus.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Babies blink significantly less often than adults, averaging only 2 to 3 times per minute.

name: Crying and Tears
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 macro view of glistening crystal emotional tears welling from the lacrimal gland and rolling down a cheek.
core_traits: Secretion of clear fluid from the lacrimal glands located in the upper outer orbit of each eye
Three distinct biological types of tears: basal (lubricating), reflex (flushing irritants like onions), and psychic (emotional)
Emotional crying is a uniquely human biological behavior accompanied by autonomic vocal sobs and weeping
Drains through tiny lacrimal puncta into the nasolacrimal duct directly into the nasal cavity

facts_and_myths.claim: Emotional psychic tears have a different biochemical composition than tears caused by chopping onions.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Emotional tears contain significantly higher concentrations of stress hormones, prolactin, and natural opioid pain relievers (leucine-enkephalin).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Your nose runs when you cry because excess tears drain directly into your nasal cavity via the nasolacrimal ducts.

facts_and_myths.claim: Newborn human babies cry actual liquid puddles of tears from the moment they are born.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Infants scream and wail at birth, but their lacrimal glands produce only enough moisture to lubricate the eye; actual tears don't flow until 2 to 8 weeks.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Crocodile tears refers to insincere grief, based on the myth that crocodiles weep while eating their prey.

name: Sweating
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 macro view of beaded sweat droplets glistening on skin evaporating under warm sunlight to cool the body.
core_traits: Release of watery saline fluid from dermal sweat glands onto the skin surface
Primary physiological mechanism for thermoregulation in humans, cooling the body via evaporative heat loss
Initiated when preoptic hypothalamic neurons detect elevated core blood temperature or ambient heat
Can also be triggered emotionally (cold sweat) by sympathetic adrenaline release on palms, soles, and armpits

facts_and_myths.claim: Humans are the most efficient evaporative sweat-cooling mammals on the entire planet.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Our naked skin packed with millions of eccrine sweat glands allowed ancestral humans to run prey to heat exhaustion (persistence hunting).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Anhydrotic people born without functioning sweat glands must avoid all intense exercise, as they can quickly die of heatstroke.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sweating heavily burns significant body fat and leads to permanent weight loss.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sweating loses water weight and electrolytes, not adipose fat; the lost weight is regained completely as soon as you drink fluids.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Spicy food induces gustatory sweating because capsaicin tricks facial heat receptors into thinking your body is overheating.

name: Shivering
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 thermal anatomical visual of skeletal muscles vibrating rapidly across the torso generating heat plumes in icy blue weather.
core_traits: Involuntary rhythmic shaking and rapid oscillating contractions of skeletal muscles in response to cold
Key thermoregulatory mechanism triggered by the preoptic area of the hypothalamus when body core temperature drops
Converts metabolic chemical energy from ATP directly into thermal body heat with high efficiency
Can increase human metabolic resting heat production by up to four to five times

facts_and_myths.claim: Shivering can elevate your body's internal heat production by as much as 500 percent.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Rapid micro-contractions (up to 250 per minute) bypass voluntary movement, converting nearly all glucose and ATP energy into friction and heat.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Teeth chattering during cold is simply the masseter jaw muscles participating in the systemic shivering reflex.

facts_and_myths.claim: Shivering is a voluntary movement that humans can easily suppress for hours during severe hypothermia.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Shivering is an involuntary autonomic survival response; when severe hypothermia sets in (core temp below 32 degrees Celsius), shivering stops completely.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When shivering suddenly stops in a freezing person without warming up, it signals a critical medical emergency: profound hypothermia.

name: Goosebumps
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 macro perspective of tiny skin bumps rising as microscopic arrector pili muscles pull hair shafts upright.
core_traits: Temporary formation of tiny raised bumps on the skin when body hairs stand erect (piloerection)
Triggered by the contraction of microscopic smooth muscle bands called arrector pili muscles
Sympathetic nervous response stimulated by cold ambient temperatures, intense fear, or awe-inspiring music
Evolutionary vestigial reflex that once fluffed dense ancestral fur to trap insulating air or intimidate predators

facts_and_myths.claim: Getting goosebumps while listening to emotionally powerful music is a scientifically recognized brain phenomenon.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Musical frisson triggers a dopamine release in the striatum and sympathetic surges, causing goosebumps across the arms and neck.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Porcupines use the exact same arrector pili piloerection reflex to stand their sharp quills upright when threatened.

facts_and_myths.claim: Human goosebumps effectively warm our modern bodies by trapping a thick layer of warm air.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because modern humans evolved fine vellus hair instead of thick fur coats, goosebumps provide virtually zero thermal insulation today.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The medical term cutis anserina comes from the Latin word for 'goose skin', describing its resemblance to a plucked bird.

name: Sleep
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 tranquil visualization of a sleeping brain shifting into slow delta brainwaves with cellular glymphatic cleaning active.
core_traits: Naturally recurring state of altered consciousness, suspended sensory activity, and reduced voluntary muscle activity
Essential for cognitive functioning, memory consolidation, cellular repair, and metabolic metabolic clearance
Governed by two interacting forces: homeostatic sleep pressure (adenosine accumulation) and circadian rhythms (melatonin)
Alternates through repeating 90-minute cycles of Non-REM sleep (stages N1, N2, N3) and REM sleep

facts_and_myths.claim: During deep sleep, the brain activates a waste-clearance system to flush out toxic amyloid plaques.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The glymphatic system pumps cerebrospinal fluid through brain tissue during sleep, washing away metabolic wastes linked to Alzheimer's.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Randy Gardner holds the scientific record for staying awake the longest under medical supervision: 11 days and 25 minutes in 1964.

facts_and_myths.claim: Adults can easily train themselves to function optimally on only 4 hours of sleep every night.
facts_and_myths.explanation: True short-sleepers with the rare DEC2 genetic mutation make up less than 1 percent of humans; chronic 4-hour sleep impairs health and memory.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Caffeine keeps you awake by plugging into adenosine receptors, blocking your brain from sensing how tired it really is.

name: REM Sleep
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 dream-like visual showing rapid darting eye movements beneath closed lids while the body remains safely in deep muscular atonia.
core_traits: Unique phase of mammalian sleep characterized by rapid, random eye movements and high brainwave activity
Stage in which the vast majority of vivid, narrative-driven dreams occur
Features skeletal muscle atonia - temporary physiological motor paralysis preventing acting out dreams
Accounts for approximately 20 to 25 percent of total adult sleep time, occurring every 90 minutes

facts_and_myths.claim: During REM sleep, your brain is almost as metabolically active as when you are fully awake.
facts_and_myths.explanation: EEG brainwave traces during REM show low-voltage, fast desynchronized waves resembling alert wakefulness, earning it the name 'paradoxical sleep'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The only skeletal muscles not paralyzed during REM atonia are the diaphragm (so you keep breathing) and extraocular eye muscles.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sleepwalking occurs exclusively during the peak height of REM sleep dreaming.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because REM features complete muscular paralysis, sleepwalking occurs during deep slow-wave Non-REM (N3) sleep when muscles can move.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) occurs when the brainstem fails to paralyze muscles, causing sleepers to violently act out nightmares.

name: Dreaming
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical 9:16 surreal artwork of neural dreamscapes swirling through glowing synaptic corridors of memory and emotion.
core_traits: Universal succession of images, ideas, emotions, and sensations occurring involuntarily during sleep
Most intense, emotionally vivid, and narrative dreams occur during Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep
Driven by activity in the amygdala, visual association cortex, and hippocampus, while the prefrontal logic center is subdued
Aids in emotional regulation, creative problem solving, memory consolidation, and threat simulation

facts_and_myths.claim: Humans forget approximately 95 to 99 percent of all their dreams within ten minutes of waking up.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Neurochemical shifts upon waking - specifically low norepinephrine in the hippocampus - prevent short-term dream memories from consolidating.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In 'lucid dreaming', the prefrontal cortex reactivates, allowing the dreamer to become aware they are dreaming and control the dream.

facts_and_myths.claim: People who claim they 'never dream' possess brains that never generate oneiric mental images.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Virtually all healthy humans dream multiple times every night; people who say they don't dream simply fail to recall them upon waking.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Before color television became common in the 1950s, studies showed a majority of people reported dreaming in black and white.

name: Immune Response
visual_anchor: Microscopic vertical 9:16 cinematic war zone of antibodies tagging spiked viruses while phagocytes engulf pathogens in glowing lymphatic lymph.
core_traits: Coordinated systemic defense mechanism protecting the human host from pathogens, toxins, and tumor cells
Composed of innate immunity (immediate, non-specific: barriers, phagocytes) and adaptive immunity (delayed, antigen-specific: B and T cells)
Generates immunological memory that enables rapid, overwhelming responses upon secondary pathogen exposure
Features cellular signaling proteins called cytokines that orchestrate fever, inflammation, and cellular recruitment

facts_and_myths.claim: Vaccines work by training the adaptive immune response using harmless antigens to build memory cells.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Vaccines expose the immune system to dead pathogens or antigens, producing memory B and T cells that neutralize future infections instantly.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Smallpox is the only infectious human disease to be completely eradicated from the face of the Earth through global vaccination.

facts_and_myths.claim: Autoimmune diseases occur because the immune system becomes excessively weak and sluggish.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Autoimmunity is a loss of self-tolerance where an overactive immune system mistakenly identifies the body's own tissues as foreign targets.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fever is an intentional immune response: higher temperatures inhibit viral replication and boost white blood cell activity.

name: Wound Healing
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 microscopic time-lapse render of a skin laceration: fibrin clotting, macrophage cleaning, and fibroblasts weaving golden collagen scars.
core_traits: Complex, highly orchestrated biological process that restores cellular structure and tissue integrity following injury
Progresses through four overlapping phases: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and tissue remodeling
Platelets initiate clotting, macrophages clear cellular debris, and fibroblasts synthesize new collagen scaffolding
Concludes with the formation of durable, fibrous scar tissue that regains up to 80 percent of original tensile strength

facts_and_myths.claim: Mature scar tissue never recovers 100 percent of the original unwounded skin's tensile strength.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because healed collagen fibers align in parallel cross-linked bundles rather than a natural basketweave, scars max out at about 80% strength.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Scars do not contain hair follicles or sweat glands because those specialized skin appendages cannot regenerate in scar tissue.

facts_and_myths.claim: Letting a wound air out dry and form a thick crusty scab makes it heal faster with less scarring.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Clinical studies prove wounds heal twice as fast with less scarring when kept in a clean, moist environment under a sterile dressing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fetuses can heal from surgery inside the first two trimesters of pregnancy with completely scarless tissue regeneration.

name: Fingerprints
visual_anchor: Vertical 9:16 macro perspective of human fingertip friction ridges swirling in illuminated loops, whorls, and arches with sweating pores.
core_traits: Raised friction ridges formed on the epidermal surfaces of fingertips, palms, and soles
Classified into three classic dermatoglyphic pattern groups: loops (60%), whorls (35%), and arches (5%)
Formed during the tenth to seventeenth weeks of fetal development inside the womb
Provides mechanical tactile friction for grasping and enhances fine micro-vibrational texture perception

facts_and_myths.claim: Identical twins share identical DNA but possess completely different, unique fingerprints.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fingerprint patterns are determined by intrauterine micro-forces like amniotic fluid currents, umbilical length, and blood pressure variations.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Koalas have friction ridges with loops and whorls so identical to human fingerprints that they can confuse crime scene investigators.

facts_and_myths.claim: Burning or slicing your fingertips with sandpaper can permanently erase your fingerprints forever.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Unless damage penetrates deep into the dermal stratum basale layer, ridges regrow in their exact original genetic configuration.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Adermatoglyphia, also called 'immigration delay disease', is an extremely rare genetic mutation that leaves people with completely smooth fingertips.
